questions.title: ISA versus implementation
questions.question: Which belongs to the ISA?
questions.explanation: The ISA defines instruction effects. Cache capacity and clock frequency are implementation choices.

questions.title: Machine state
questions.question: What does RIP represent?
questions.explanation: RIP tracks instruction execution. RSP points at the stack; RAX is a general-purpose register commonly used for returns.

questions.title: Values are made of bytes
questions.question: An 8-byte long begins at address 0x100. Which addresses does it occupy?
questions.explanation: Addresses count bytes. Eight bytes occupy offsets 0 through 7.

questions.title: Assembly versus machine code
questions.question: What does an assembler primarily produce?
options: Only a list of C variable names
questions.explanation: Assembly is text describing instructions. The assembler encodes it; linking resolves connections between object files.

questions.title: Decode the lecture’s store
questions.question: The bytes 48 89 03 encode movq %rax,(%rbx). What is 0x40059e in the slide?
options: The value being stored from RAX
The destination data address in RBX
The address where the instruction bytes are stored
questions.explanation: Code bytes have addresses too. The operand (%rbx) separately selects the data address. This instruction is three bytes long; q describes its eight-byte data transfer.

questions.title: Read object code
questions.question: Which tool command disassembles an executable named sum?
questions.explanation: objdump -d displays disassembled executable sections. In GDB, disassemble sum shows the named function; x/14xb sum examines 14 raw bytes. Disassembly does not reconstruct the original C exactly.

questions.title: Avoid overgeneralizing
questions.question: Which statement is reliable?
options: CISC/RISC alone does not determine speed or power
Every RISC instruction in every ISA has the same length
x86 instructions never exceed eight bytes
questions.explanation: Implementation, workload and encoding details matter. x86 permits instructions up to 15 bytes; some RISC ISAs offer compressed encodings.

questions.title: Copy a long without truncation
questions.cCode:
// long A, B;
B = A;
questions.hint: Use an eight-byte load and store.
questions.explanation: movq reads all eight bytes of A into RAX, then writes eight bytes to B. A must stay unchanged. The large case detects accidental 32-bit truncation and JavaScript precision loss.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Return a full-width constant
questions.cCode: unsigned long marker(void) { return 0x123456789abcdef0UL; }
questions.hint: Use $ for the hexadecimal constant and RAX for the result.
questions.explanation: A register-destination movq can carry a full 64-bit immediate. Most other q instructions accept only a sign-extended 32-bit immediate. ret returns to the supplied caller.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Replace only the low byte
questions.cCode:
// Machine-level update: RAX contains x.
// Replace bits 0–7 with 0x5a; preserve all other bits.
questions.hint: Use the byte alias, not the full register.
questions.explanation: AL is the low byte of RAX. A byte write preserves bits 8–63; writing EAX would clear the upper 32 bits.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Replace the low word
questions.cCode: // RAX contains x. Replace bits 0–15 with 0x1234.
questions.hint: Use AX with the w suffix.
questions.explanation: AX selects the low 16 bits. A word is two bytes in x86 terminology.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: How large is q?
questions.question: How many bytes does movq transfer?
questions.explanation: q means quadword: four two-byte words = eight bytes. It does not specify instruction length.

questions.title: What is AX?
questions.question: Which part of RAX is AX?
questions.explanation: RAX/EAX/AX/AL are overlapping views, not independent storage.

questions.title: A 32-bit write
questions.question: After movq $-1,%rax; movl $1,%eax, what is RAX?
questions.explanation: The EAX write clears RAX bits 32–63.

questions.title: Identify an immediate
questions.question: Which operand is the numeric constant 42?
questions.explanation: $42 is an immediate. Bare 42 refers to memory at address 42; %42 is not a register.

questions.title: C long versus l
questions.question: Under Linux x86-64 LP64, which suffix copies a C long?
questions.explanation: LP64 makes long and pointers 64-bit. Other ABIs can differ; the lab states its data model.

questions.title: An illegal move
questions.question: Why is movq A,B invalid for this exercise?
options: q cannot be used with variables
questions.explanation: The ordinary mov form cannot copy directly between two memory operands. Load A into a register, then store to B.

questions.title: Read through a pointer
questions.cCode: long read_value(long *p) { return *p; }
questions.hint: Dereference RDI using parentheses.
questions.explanation: RDI is the address, and (%rdi) is the eight-byte value at that address. Load into the return register, then return.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Write through a pointer
questions.cCode: void store(long *p, long x) { *p = x; }
questions.hint: Put the parenthesized pointer last.
questions.explanation: The source is RSI, the destination is memory at RDI. This function returns no value but must return correctly.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Copy between pointees
questions.cCode: void copy(long *dst, long *src) { *dst = *src; }
questions.hint: Use a temporary register between the two memory locations.
questions.explanation: The load saves *src in RAX. The store writes that value to *dst. The source memory must remain unchanged.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Swap two longs, including aliases
questions.hint: Save both values before overwriting either pointee.
questions.explanation: RAX preserves the old *xp while RDX captures the old *yp. Only after both loads do the stores occur. The alias case confirms that xp == yp is safe.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Address or value?
questions.question: RDI=0x100 and memory[0x100]=23. What does movq %rdi,%rax copy?
questions.explanation: Without parentheses it copies the register’s address value. Registers themselves do not have normal memory addresses.

questions.title: Dereference
questions.question: RDI=0x100 and memory[0x100]=23. What does movq (%rdi),%rax copy?
questions.explanation: Parentheses tell mov to read memory at the address in RDI.

questions.title: Store direction
questions.question: Which stores RAX to the address in RDX?
questions.explanation: AT&T destination is last. Parentheses on the destination make it a memory store.

questions.title: Why a temporary?
questions.question: Why not perform *xp=*yp; *yp=*xp; as a swap?
options: The first assignment destroys the original *xp
questions.explanation: The second load sees the already-overwritten value. Preserve the original before the store.

questions.title: Load a long array element
questions.cCode: long get(long *a, long i) { return a[i]; }
questions.hint: Use RDI as base and RSI as index.
questions.explanation: The index is multiplied by sizeof(long)=8. movq dereferences that address and returns the selected element.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Load an int with a 64-bit address
questions.cCode: int get(int *a, long i) { return a[i]; }
questions.hint: Data width and address-register width are different decisions.
questions.explanation: int is four bytes, so scale 4 and movl match. The return is checked in EAX because the declared result is int. Address registers are still 64-bit.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Store into a long array
questions.cCode: void set(long *a, long i, long v) { a[i] = v; }
questions.hint: Only one array element is an output.
questions.explanation: RDX is the third argument. Compute the selected element address and store; other elements are checked for preservation.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Combine an index and displacement
questions.cCode: long next(long *a, long i) { return a[i+1]; }
questions.hint: Expand (i+1)*8.
questions.explanation: 8*i accounts for i elements; the extra displacement 8 accounts for one more long.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Compute an address
questions.question: RDX=0xf000, RCX=0x100. What address is 8(%rdx,%rcx,4)?
questions.explanation: 0xf000 + 0x100×4 + 8 = 0xf408. This computes an address, not the memory contents.

questions.title: Omitted base
questions.question: RDX=0xf000. What is 0x80(,%rdx,2)?
questions.explanation: There is no base register. The address is 0x80 + 2×0xf000.

questions.title: Legal scales
questions.question: Which scale is invalid in an x86 address?
questions.explanation: The hardware encoding permits 1, 2, 4 and 8. To compute 9*x, use x + 8*x.

questions.title: Little endian
questions.question: An eight-byte value is 0x1122334455667788. Which byte is stored first?
questions.explanation: The low-order byte occupies the lowest memory address.

questions.title: Correct slide 35’s register sizes
questions.question: Which is a valid 64-bit address for a four-byte array element?
questions.explanation: Use matching address-register widths. The scale remains 4 for int, regardless of the 64-bit registers.

questions.title: Return an element address
questions.cCode: long *element(long *a, long i) { return &a[i]; }
questions.hint: Use lea, not a load.
questions.explanation: The test supplies an address but no array data, so an accidental mov fails. lea computes the pointer without a memory access.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Multiply by nine with LEA
questions.cCode: long times9(long x) { return x*9; }
questions.explanation: Use the same register as base and index: x+8*x. The x86 address calculation wraps to 64 bits; these C test values avoid signed overflow.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Compute x + 4*y + 12
questions.cCode: long combine(long x, long y) { return x + 4*y + 12; }
questions.hint: Map each arithmetic term onto one address component.
questions.explanation: Displacement=12, base=x, index=y and scale=4 match the expression directly. No memory is read.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Build 12*x in two stages
questions.cCode: long times12(long x) { return x*12; }
questions.hint: First compute three times x; then multiply by four.
questions.explanation: lea computes 3*x. salq shifts the bit pattern left by two, producing 12*x for these representable inputs. This is a machine translation of multiplication; it does not require writing a negative signed left shift in C.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: LEA or MOV?
questions.question: RDX=0x100, RCX=4, memory[0x110]=8. leaq (%rdx,%rcx,4),%rax gives?
questions.explanation: lea computes 0x100+4×4. movq with the same source would load 8.

questions.title: Does LEA need allocated memory?
questions.question: Why can LEA compute an address where no test memory is allocated?
options: It reads zero from missing memory
questions.explanation: No dereference happens. A later load/store would require a valid allocated address.

questions.title: Lecture self-check
questions.question: Which computes RAX=9*RDI without a memory read?
questions.explanation: The legal scale 8 plus the base gives nine times the input. movq would dereference; scale 9 is invalid.

questions.title: Preserved flags
questions.question: After cmpq, does leaq change the flags used by a branch?
options: Yes, it sets ZF from its result
questions.explanation: lea and mov preserve flags; add and sub update them.

questions.title: Return x minus y
questions.cCode: long difference(long x,long y) { return x-y; }
questions.hint: The destination supplies the left side of subtraction.
questions.explanation: Copy the minuend x, then subtract y. AT&T operand order matters for sub.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Multiply two longs
questions.cCode: long product(long x,long y) { return x*y; }
questions.hint: Use the two-operand imul form.
questions.explanation: Copy x into RAX and multiply by y. The cases include zero, a negative result and a value beyond signed 32-bit range.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Correct translation of slide 33’s C
questions.hint: Compute 5*y, not 2*x+4.
questions.explanation: RAX accumulates x+y+z. RCX gets y+4*y. Multiply those two values. The unused t3 and t4 in the slide C have no effect on the result.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Translate what the slide assembly actually does
questions.hint: Trace data dependencies rather than variable names in the C column.
questions.explanation: leaq 4(%rdi,%rdi),%rcx computes 4+x+x. The original 48*y calculation is dead: removing it does not change the returned value.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Subtraction direction
questions.question: What does subq %rsi,%rax compute?
questions.explanation: AT&T destination is last and is also an input to two-operand subtraction.

questions.title: C versus assembly
questions.question: Which statement about signed C overflow is correct?
options: It is undefined; assembly wraparound does not make it valid C
C signed arithmetic always wraps identically to x86
questions.explanation: The machine has fixed-width bit behavior. C’s language rules are a separate contract.

questions.title: Spot the slide mismatch
questions.question: Which expression does slide 33’s final imul use as its second factor?
questions.explanation: The live RCX value comes from leaq 4(%rdi,%rdi). RDX’s 48*y value is not used by that imul.

questions.title: Extract the low byte
questions.cCode: unsigned long bits(unsigned long x) { return x & 0xffUL; }
questions.hint: Copy x, then apply the appropriate mask.
questions.explanation: The mask operation implements x & 0xffUL. Cases exercise zero, a set bit, a clear bit, and upper bits that must not be lost.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Set bit 3
questions.cCode: unsigned long bits(unsigned long x) { return x | 8UL; }
questions.hint: Copy x, then apply the appropriate mask.
questions.explanation: The mask operation implements x | 8UL. Cases exercise zero, a set bit, a clear bit, and upper bits that must not be lost.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Clear bit 3
questions.cCode: unsigned long bits(unsigned long x) { return x & ~8UL; }
questions.hint: Copy x, then apply the appropriate mask.
questions.explanation: The mask operation implements x & ~8UL. Cases exercise zero, a set bit, a clear bit, and upper bits that must not be lost.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Toggle bit 3
questions.cCode: unsigned long bits(unsigned long x) { return x ^ 8UL; }
questions.hint: Copy x, then apply the appropriate mask.
questions.explanation: The mask operation implements x ^ 8UL. Cases exercise zero, a set bit, a clear bit, and upper bits that must not be lost.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Complement every bit
questions.cCode: unsigned long invert(unsigned long x) { return ~x; }
questions.hint: NOT has one operand.
questions.explanation: NOT flips all 64 bits and preserves flags. The unsigned result is compared as a bit pattern, even when the signed display is negative.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Return whether bit 3 is set
questions.cCode: int has_bit(unsigned long x) { return (x & 8UL) != 0; }
questions.hint: Use test and a conditional branch; return 0 or 1.
solutions:
movl $0,%eax
testq $8,%rdi
je done
movl $1,%eax
done: ret
questions.explanation: Initialize the return to false. test leaves x intact and sets ZF according to x&8. If nonzero, return true.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: AND truth rule
questions.question: What is 0b1010 & 0b1100?
questions.explanation: Only bit 3 is one in both operands.

questions.title: XOR truth rule
questions.question: What is 0b1010 ^ 0b1100?
questions.explanation: XOR marks differing bit positions.

questions.title: Choose a clear mask
questions.question: Which C expression always clears bit 5?
questions.explanation: AND with a zero in bit 5 clears it; other mask bits are one and preserve x.

questions.title: Bitwise is not logical
questions.question: For x=2 and y=4, what are x&y and x&&y?
questions.explanation: Bitwise AND finds no shared set bit; logical AND sees two nonzero values.

questions.title: TEST side effects
questions.question: What does testq $8,%rax change?
questions.explanation: It computes an AND for flags but discards the numeric result.

questions.title: Shift left with wraparound
questions.cCode: unsigned long times8(unsigned long x) { return x << 3; }
questions.hint: Copy x, then shift by an immediate count.
questions.explanation: SHL/SAL inserts three zeros and discards the high three bits. Unsigned C matches this wrapping behavior for a valid count.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Unsigned right shift
questions.cCode: unsigned long half(unsigned long x) { return x >> 1; }
questions.hint: Treat the input as unsigned.
questions.explanation: SHR fills with zero. Upper-bit cases distinguish it from SAR.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Arithmetic right shift
questions.cCode:
// x86 arithmetic right shift semantics for signed x
long shifted(long x) { return x >> 2; }
questions.hint: Preserve the sign bit.
questions.explanation: SAR replicates the sign bit. For -7 the result is -2, which differs from C -7/4 = -1. This exercise explicitly assumes arithmetic signed right-shift behavior.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Shift by a runtime count
questions.cCode:
// Precondition: 0 <= k < 64
unsigned long shift(unsigned long x,unsigned long k) { return x << k; }
questions.hint: Use RCX/CL for the count.
questions.explanation: The second argument arrives in RSI, but the shift encoding requires CL. Move RSI to RCX, then use its low-byte alias for the count.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Extract a four-bit field
questions.cCode: unsigned long field(unsigned long x) { return (x >> 8) & 15UL; }
questions.hint: Shift first, mask second.
questions.explanation: First move bits 8–11 into positions 0–3. Then mask out every other bit. Reversing those operations would erase the field too early.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: SAL versus SHL
questions.question: How do salq and shlq differ in result?
options: SHL only works on unsigned registers
They do not; they are synonyms
SAL preserves the sign on a left shift
questions.explanation: Registers have bit patterns, not signed types. Both left-shift identically.

questions.title: Negative right shift
questions.question: What is arithmetic -7 shifted right by one?
questions.explanation: SAR rounds the mathematical quotient down; signed C division truncates toward zero.

questions.title: Variable count register
questions.question: Which is a valid variable-count shift?
questions.explanation: Only CL supplies a variable shift count in these x86 forms.

questions.title: Hardware versus C
questions.question: What does x86 shlq $64,%rax do to RAX?
questions.explanation: The low six count bits are zero. This is not a valid translation of an unrestricted C x<<64, which has an out-of-range count.

questions.title: Undefined overflow flag
questions.question: After shlq $2,%rax, can jo reliably test signed overflow?
options: No; OF is undefined for that count
questions.explanation: Only count one defines OF for these shifts. The checker refuses to guess it.

questions.title: Signed maximum
questions.cCode: long max(long x,long y) { return x>y ? x:y; }
questions.hint: Default to one result, then conditionally replace it.
solutions:
movq %rsi,%rax
cmpq %rsi,%rdi
jle done
movq %rdi,%rax
done: ret
questions.explanation: The minimum signed input forces subtraction overflow; jle still works because it uses SF and OF correctly.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Unsigned maximum
questions.cCode: unsigned long max(unsigned long x,unsigned long y) { return x>y ? x:y; }
questions.hint: Compare the same way, but choose the unsigned branch family.
solutions:
movq %rsi,%rax
cmpq %rsi,%rdi
jbe done
movq %rdi,%rax
done: ret
questions.explanation: jbe is unsigned below-or-equal. A signed branch would misclassify the all-ones input as negative.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Sum a long array
questions.hint: Use a top-tested loop and scale 8.
solutions:
xorq %rax,%rax
xorq %rcx,%rcx
loop: cmpq %rsi,%rcx
jge done
addq (%rdi,%rcx,8),%rax
incq %rcx
jmp loop
done: ret
questions.explanation: Initialize sum and index to zero. Check i>=n before accessing memory. Accumulate a[i], increment, and repeat. n=0 must not read an element.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: CMP direction
questions.question: After cmpq %rsi,%rdi, which comparison does jg express?
questions.explanation: cmp calculates RDI-RSI for flags. jg interprets the relation as signed.

questions.title: High-bit comparison
questions.question: For RAX=0xffffffffffffffff, cmpq $1,%rax followed by ja will…
questions.explanation: As unsigned, all ones is 2^64-1, above 1. Signed jg would not branch.

questions.title: Zero iterations
questions.question: Why test a while condition before the body?
options: The loop may need to execute zero times
It always makes the program faster
questions.explanation: A bottom-tested loop executes at least once, which changes the C semantics.

questions.title: Save and restore with the stack
questions.cCode:
// RDI contains x. Save it on the stack, set RDI to 99,
// then recover the original x into RAX. Finish with balanced RSP.
questions.hint: Push the original before the overwrite.
questions.explanation: push captures the original value before it is overwritten. pop retrieves it into RAX and restores the stack pointer.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Reverse two values with PUSH/POP
questions.cCode: // RDI=x, RSI=y. Use two pushes and two pops to exchange them.
questions.hint: Read the pushes in reverse order when planning the pops.
questions.explanation: After both pushes y is on top. The first pop gets y; the second gets x. Both stack slots are released.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Use a frame for a local long
questions.hint: Restore RSP to RBP before popping RBP.
solutions:
pushq %rbp
movq %rsp,%rbp
subq $16,%rsp
movq %rdi,-8(%rbp)
movq -8(%rbp),%rax
addq $1,%rax
leave
ret
questions.explanation: Save the caller’s RBP, establish the frame, reserve local space, store and reload t, then add one. leave releases local storage and restores RBP. ret then consumes the return address.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: PUSH stack movement
questions.question: RSP=0x8000. After pushq %rax, where is the value?
questions.explanation: The stack grows toward lower addresses, by eight bytes for pushq.

questions.title: POP stack movement
questions.question: RSP=0x7ff0. After popq %rax, what is RSP?
questions.explanation: The value at the old top is loaded, then RSP advances eight bytes.

questions.title: Who initializes the stack?
questions.question: Must each C function initialize a brand-new stack before using push?
options: No; it receives an existing stack from its caller/runtime
Yes; push has no stack until the function creates one
No; push stores inside the CPU only
questions.explanation: The stack is memory addressed by RSP. A function must use and restore the supplied stack correctly.

questions.title: POP does not erase
questions.question: Does popq erase the bytes it reads?
options: Only if it pops into RAX
No; it changes RSP and its destination
questions.explanation: Deallocation changes which bytes are live, not their physical contents.

questions.title: Why RET fails
questions.question: What happens if a saved register remains above the return address when ret executes?
options: RET returns the saved value through RAX
RET uses those saved bits as the return address
questions.explanation: RET only pops its target; it does not understand your frame layout.

questions.title: Write a leaf function
questions.cCode: long plus(long x,long y) { return x+y; }
questions.hint: A simple leaf can consist of a calculation and ret.
questions.explanation: A leaf function makes no other calls. It needs neither a local frame nor a saved register here: compute in RAX and return.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Call a helper and use its result
questions.hint: Balance the alignment adjustment around call.
solutions:
caller:
subq $8,%rsp
call plus
addq $8,%rsp
addq $1,%rax
ret
plus:
leaq (%rdi,%rsi),%rax
ret
questions.explanation: Reserve eight bytes to align the caller’s stack, call plus, release the reservation, and add one to its RAX return value. The helper’s ret resumes inside caller.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Complete slide 15: sumstore
questions.hint: Save RBX, put dest there, call, store through RBX, restore RBX.
solutions:
sumstore:
pushq %rbx
movq %rdx,%rbx
call plus
movq %rax,(%rbx)
popq %rbx
ret
plus:
leaq (%rdi,%rsi),%rax
movq $123,%rdx
ret
questions.explanation: RBX safely carries the destination across plus because it is callee-saved. The explicit RDX clobber exposes the bug in keeping dest in a caller-saved register. push/pop preserve the original RBX and maintain call alignment.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Nested calls with a saved input
questions.hint: Preserve both the caller’s RBX and your own x.
solutions:
outer:
pushq %rbx
movq %rdi,%rbx
call twice
addq %rbx,%rax
popq %rbx
ret
twice:
leaq (%rdi,%rdi),%rax
movq $0,%rdi
ret
questions.explanation: Save x in a callee-saved register before calling twice. RDI is caller-saved and deliberately clobbered. Add the preserved original x to the helper’s result, restore RBX and return.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: CALL’s saved value
questions.question: What does call push?
questions.explanation: call saves where to resume. The callee later supplies its result through the ABI’s return register.

questions.title: RET versus RAX
questions.question: Which action returns a long value 7 correctly?
questions.explanation: The numeric result and return address are different things. Pushing 7 before ret would redirect control to address 7 on a real machine.

questions.title: Argument mapping
questions.question: Where does the third integer/pointer argument arrive under this ABI?
questions.explanation: The order is RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9.

questions.title: Register preservation
questions.question: Which register must a callee restore if it changes it?
questions.explanation: RBX is callee-saved. RAX and RDI may be clobbered; callers must preserve live values themselves.

questions.title: Alignment before a call
questions.question: RSP is 0x7ff8 on entry. What does pushq %rbx do for the next call?
options: It has no effect on alignment
questions.explanation: The eight-byte push changes entry alignment to the standard pre-call alignment.

questions.title: Why save dest?
questions.question: Why does sumstore move RDX into RBX before calling plus?
options: RDX may be clobbered by plus
RDX cannot be used in an address
questions.explanation: dest must survive the call. sumstore also preserves the caller’s original RBX with push/pop.

questions.title: Read an array and extract a field
questions.cCode: unsigned long field(unsigned long *a,long i) { return (a[i] >> 8) & 255UL; }
questions.hint: Separate address calculation from value manipulation.
questions.explanation: Use scale 8 for the unsigned-long array, load the value, logically shift, and mask. LEA alone would return an address instead of the field.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Set a bit chosen at runtime
questions.cCode:
// 0 <= k < 64
unsigned long set(unsigned long x,unsigned long k) { return x | (1UL<<k); }
questions.hint: Build the mask in a q register.
questions.explanation: Build a 64-bit mask starting at 1, shift it by CL, then OR it with x. The k=63 case checks that the mask is not accidentally only 32 bits wide.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Call, save a destination and store masked data
questions.hint: This combines sumstore’s structure with bit-field extraction.
solutions:
write_field:
pushq %rbx
movq %rsi,%rbx
call extract
movq %rax,(%rbx)
popq %rbx
ret
extract:
movq %rdi,%rax
shrq $4,%rax
andq $255,%rax
ret
questions.explanation: Save out in RBX across extract, preserve the incoming RBX, and call with aligned RSP. The helper returns a field in RAX; the caller stores it through the saved pointer.
questions.dataModel: x86-64 / LP64: long and pointers 8 bytes; int 4 bytes

questions.title: Find the first wrong idea
questions.question: A solution uses leaq (%rdi,%rsi,8),%rax for return a[i]. What is wrong?
options: It returns the address, not the element
questions.explanation: Use movq for a[i], lea for &a[i].

questions.title: What does passing mean?
questions.question: All listed tests pass. What can you conclude?
options: The code is a complete native executable
The tested inputs satisfy the checked outputs and preservation rules
The solution is correct for every possible input
questions.explanation: Tests give evidence, not a universal proof. The bounded interpreter also does not emit machine code.

questions.title: A translation checklist
questions.question: Which should you decide before choosing movl or movq?
options: The data type width in the stated ABI
The number of characters in the variable name
Whether the value happens to be small today
questions.explanation: The declared representation determines width. A long still needs eight bytes even when its current value is 1.
